newsitem.title: UK: Sugar trade gets new book after 30 year wait.
newsitem.headline: Sugar trade gets new book after 30 year wait.

text.p: The world of sugar, unique among commodities for its sheer diversity of production and development, can now boast a belated but comprehensive addition to its literature after a wait of nearly 30 years.

The last detailed analysis of the global sugar industry was published in 1957 and an update was long overdue on a staple commodity, which is consumed in some shape or form in every country of the world.

Sugar is one of the most important soft commodities in world trade and also one the world's largest provider of calories, according to a new book called "The International Sugar Trade" written by Tony Hannah and Donald Spence.
Hannah is chief economist at the London-based International Sugar Organisation, while Spence is a former floor trader who then turned his hand to research at trade house E D & F Man.
"Sugar is such a complex commodity, it is so political," Hannah said in an interview.
"It's one of the most autarchic commodities, everybody wants to be self-sufficient in sugar. It's also unique because it comes from entirely different plants," Hannah said.

Sugar cane, which accounts for the lion's share of world sugar production, has been cultivated for thousands of years, although the presence of sugar in red and white beet plants was not discovered until the 18th century.

Hannah said sugar acted as the economic mainstay in many developing countries, which tend to benefit from the hot and moist environment needed to grow cane, the most efficient collector of solar energy in the plant kingdom.
Beet, which is usually rotated with wheat and barley, is limited exclusively to temperate zones but can be cultivated under a wide range of natural conditions.

"Sugar is a very good development vehicle. It's got an industrial and agricultural side, that's fairly unique in commodities," Hannah said. "It gives more employment, especially in developing countries."

The book gives an in-depth analysis of all aspects of the world sugar trade, from the history of cane to swings in the supply/demand equation and prospects following the break-up of the Soviet Union and the modernisation of Cuba's sugar industry.

Key factors for the future, such as the expected accession of former Soviet Bloc countries into the European Union and the increasing market share of alternative sweeteners, receive detailed treatment.

Swings in the global list of exporters and importers are also analysed, especially as total output is increasingly dominated by a handful of major producers -- including major developing nations Brazil, India, China and Thailand.
One country among many that will play a key role in the future of the world sugar is Brazil, the world's largest exporter in 1995 and second largest single producer after India.

The Brazilian government, reeling from the first oil price shock of 1973, launched a programme in the late 1970s to produce enough alcohol from sugar cane to fuel all the country's cars. Thus cane was diverted from sugar production.
But the Brazilian alcohol sector is ailing and sales of new alcohol-powered cars are in decline.
"The major factor (for the world situation) is the future of the Brazilian alcohol programme, at least on the supply side," Hannah said.
China, which has a low per capita sugar consumption of six kg (13.2 lbs.) compared with the world average of 20 kg (44.09 lbs.), has long been considered the potential saviour of the world market.
But alternative sweeteners such as HFCS (high fructose corn syrup) are making substantial inroads in terms of market share and general statistical information is also thin on the ground.

"China is an enigma -- they're a major market factor," Hannah said, noting that while a poor crop forced China to import 3.7 million tons of sugar in 1988, it staged a remarkable recovery five years later and exported 1.56 million.
